evidence: LC nr95017968 identifies the Colgate historian born in 1965. His Bandits, Eunuchs, Ming-court and Mongol-history works carry 29/39 listed citation weights. Olynthus and the Sardes inscriptions belong to David Moore Robinson (6); Augustinian Settlement and Cistercian Abbeys belong to David Martin Robinson (4).

Nicholas Vincent's university bibliography confirms The Holy Blood, Peter des Roches, Isabella of Angouleme, The Murderers of Thomas Becket and the other medieval-English works (42/44 citation weights). The two small exceptions, Jouer pour la cite and Rome, scene ouverte, are Alexandre Vincent's works.

LC n84024703 is Jonathan David Hill. History, Power, and Identity and Rethinking History and Myth account for 15/37 citation weights. Introduction (1996) likely matches his Iowa volume's introduction, raising his share to 22/37, but is underspecified. Other titles demonstrably belong to namesakes; neither the roughly two-thirds mostly threshold nor a minority judgment is secure.

Bibliography and the Sociology of Texts, its translations, Cambridge History of the Book in Britain IV, the Stationers' apprentices lists and Making Meaning are Donald Francis McKenzie's. Identifiable bibliography and book-history works carry 55/57 citation weights. Measuring Inequality with Asset Indicators is David J. McKenzie's (1); et al is unidentifiable (1).

The key label J. W. Powell matches John Wesley Powell's Wyandot Government, Bureau of Ethnology report and related ethnological/irrigation writings, about 10/31 citation weights. The Cicero works are Jonathan G. F. Powell's (12); forestry is J. M. Powell's, House of Lords is Enoch Powell's, and Collectanea Alexandrina is John Undershell Powell's.

LC n78028725 identifies John Marshall Carter, author of Rape in Medieval England (5/35 citation weights). Suetonius and Caesar are John M. Carter's editions; Metaponto belongs to Joseph Coleman Carter; Greek Ivory-Carving and Masks of Ortheia to Jane Burr Carter; ABC for Book Collectors to the bibliographer John Carter.

LC no2021000496 identifies the Erskine historian whose CV confirms The Last Slave Ships (5/32 citation weights). Lexicon Technicum and Navigantium are the early encyclopedist's; Essays in Industry and Technology is John Raymond Harris's; Moving Rooms and Palladian Revival belong to the architectural historian. Moral Enhancement and Freedom is the bioethicist's.

David Gaunt's Familjeliv i Norden, Utbildning till statens tjanst, Holocaust, family-history and related works carry about 32/48 citation weights. Gender and Genre, Can the Middle Ages Be Postcolonial?, Cambridge Companion to Medieval French Literature and The Troubadours are Simon Gaunt's (15). Siparium in Quintilian is by D. M. Gaunt of Clifton College (1).

LC n50049263 identifies David Levering Lewis, not the authors represented here. Neither Wolf Nor Dog and the Native-American works are David Rich Lewis's (18/43 citation weights); The Good Fight and Make This Your Canada are the Canadian politician's (12). Navigation, development, classics, philosophy and science-history titles belong to further namesakes; none is identifiable as David Levering Lewis's.

John MacQueen wrote St Nynia, the Rhinns place-name study and The Enlightenment and Scottish Literature, and edited Ballatis of Luve (10/48 citation weights). The university archive explicitly assigns Atlas of Scottish History and Common Law and Feudal Society to his son Hector; Laws and Courts and the other legal works likewise belong to Hector, not John.
